The exterior of the lolwapa (small front courtyard) (left) and house of the mother of Gabarekwe Kgaga, a San woman living in Matlapaneng ward, made from tshikitshane (Stipagrostis uniplumis) grass bundles and letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) given to her by neighbours. She has woven these salvaged materials together to make walling.

The homestead of Gabarekwe Kgaga, a San woman living in Matlapaneng. She built this house using drinks cans for walling from a local bar, due to the difficulty of finding letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) at the river.

The lolwapa (small front courtyard) of Gabarekwe Kgaga, a San woman living in Matlapaneng, made from tshikitshane (Stipagrostis uniplumis) grass bundles recovered from a dilapidated neighbour's roof. She built this house using drinks cans for walling from a local bar, due to the difficulty of finding letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) at the river.

The lolwapa (small front courtyard) and house of the mother of Gabarekwe Kgaga, a San woman living in Matlapaneng ward, made from tshikitshane (Stipagrostis uniplumis) grass bundles and letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) given to her by neighbours.

Houses in the plot of Boikwatho Captain, a San woman living in Sanyedi ward. The house to the left, where her cousin lives, is falling down. The middle house is where his niece stays, and the one on the right where her husband's niece lives. The layout of the plot is unlike others in Sanyedi, with houses facing out to a path rather than into a central living space. Boikwatho explained that this was how her family built in Sehitwa, in a line facing the same direction. She claimed that this was a San tradition, but is more likely to have been a result of Mbanderu influence in Sehitwa.

View (looking northward) of buildings around the main plaza of San Felipe pueblo, with the Rio Grande river in the distance, and Santa Ana Mesa visible in the distance on the left.  In the foreground a group of villagers is gathered, and closer still to the camera the collector James Stevenson can be seen talking with a local inhabitant.  According to Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the 'dwellings of this village never reach higher than two stor[ey]s', and the 'walls of the old pueblo are constructed of well-selected lava bo[u]lders of uniform size'.  The photograph was probably taken by John Hillers from the roof of the Catholic church.
